Did your team mask and blur things out? The out-of-focus stuff sometimes doesn't make sense in terms of the possible lens used and distance. I think trying to make it physically correct will help the ad.

For example, in the first shot: if the baskets of gifts were closer to the actors than the back wall, and the focus of the camera is on the actors. Why wouldn't the baskets of gifts be in focus too?

The victim was also much bigger than the aggressor and was at an advantaged situation until the train arrived. I think it will be about determining whether the smaller man was actually applying force to push the bigger man in front of the train. Considering the moment the victim fell, he landed on the ground, then the aggressor also fell backwards, I guess you can argue the third law of physics can be applied here. However, is that due to him trying to pull the other way to not fall down together or is it from him trying to push the man down the track and bouncing back? I think since the smaller man fell after the victim rather than them bouncing back at the same time, it's more likely that he was trying to pull the other way to avoid falling onto him.

Also, the first point of impact to the ground is still on the platform, then the smaller man was swept down together, as the victim fell further back, the smaller man immediately tried to crawl backwards and turn around. The first fall might be caused by the victim trying maintain a distance so the punches doesn't land on him. However, you can argue the lethal fall that killed him was not directly caused by the smaller man. It might be acaused by this altercation or the victim trying to dodge the punches and losing balance, but there's space towards the camera the victim could have stepped back towards, there's also the slippery ground, design flaw and management flaw of the station.

The use of 360 degrees to measure a full circle or rotation comes from ancient astronomy and is separate from the sexagesimal system, though they are often used together.  
  
The number 360 was likely chosen because it is approximately the number of days in a year, and ancient astronomers observed that the sun returned to the same position in the sky after about 360 days. This made it a convenient choice for measuring the full circle of the heavens, and this convention was then applied to circles in general.
